title: Which whole answer is more likely?
hook: A model scores a whole answer by multiplying its tokens' chances. Which comes out on top?

knows: a model picks the next token from probabilities (next-word-tally)
that a whole text's probability is the product along its path (greedy-word-trap)
doesNotKnow: that because every extra token multiplies by a number below 1, the most probable whole answer is biased toward short ones, so search for the single most likely text needs a length correction

misconception: The answer whose every token the model is more confident about is the more probable answer, so 'most likely' means 'best'.
objective: The learner can explain that a 10-token answer at 85% per token (19.7%) loses to a 2-token answer at 50% per token (25%) because each extra token multiplies the whole by a number below 1, and that scoring per token removes this bias toward short answers.

claims.text: 0.5 x 0.5 = 25% and 0.85^10 = 19.7%, so the 2-token answer S is more probable than the 10-token answer L.
claims.source: Arithmetic; whole() in Demo.tsx; node 2026-10-14: 0.25 and 0.19687.

claims.text: At 85% per token, L beats S's 25% only up to 8 tokens (0.85^8 = 27.2%, 0.85^9 = 23.2%).

A whole answer's probability is the product of its tokens' probabilities, so each extra token multiplies the whole by something below 1 and can only lower it; therefore the single most probable answer tends to be a short one.
claims.source: Chain rule of probability: P(w1..wn) = product of P(wi | w1..wi-1), each factor <= 1. The toy's per-token chances are fixed and invented (stage tag 'Invented token odds').

claims.text: Scoring per token (the geometric mean of the token chances, a length-normalised score) puts L ahead: 85% against 50%, at every length.
claims.source: (p^n)^(1/n) = p: S 0.5, L 0.85 for any n. Shown on the stage as 'per token: 85% (whole: ...)'.

claims.text: Real decoders add such a length correction (length penalty or normalisation), because exact or beam search for the most probable output favours short outputs.
claims.source: Wu et al. (2016), 'Google's neural machine translation system', arXiv 1609.08144, section 7 (length normalisation in beam search); Murray and Chiang (2018), 'Correcting length bias in neural machine translation', WMT 2018. About real systems; needs the fact-checker. The brief's optional Stahlberg and Byrne (2019) sentence is not in learner text.

recall.question: A search keeps the single most probable reply, scoring each reply by multiplying its token chances. Without any correction, which kind of reply does it tend to pick?
options: Short replies, even when their tokens are less certain
Long replies, because they carry more information
Replies whose every token is the most confident
recall.why: Every extra token multiplies the whole by a number below 1, so long replies lose probability. Real decoders add a length correction, such as scoring per token.
